summary: The paper builds a lightweight agent-based simulation of a repeated human-AI decision loop to argue that sycophancy (deferring to the user's stated belief over the AI's private judgement) corrupts trust calibration only when the AI is meaningfully more competent than the user, and can actually help when the user is more competent. This revision responds to prior-round reviewer critiques by re-running the structural-constant sensitivity sweep with 10 seeds and four additional perturbed constants (previously single-seed, five constants), decomposing the equal-competence residual accuracy cost into deferred vs. non-deferred rounds (finding it's a disagreement-conditioning selection artifact converging to 0.5 accuracy, not the confidence-conditioning mechanism previously hypothesized), and adding a hedged literature-based plausibility check for the paper's core AI>user competence assumption.
strengths:
- I re-ran sim_extra3.py directly and its output reproduces the paper's §3.2 table to 2-3 decimal places (e.g. default: trust gap -0.2136±0.0065 vs. paper's -0.214±0.007; extreme-confidence row: -0.2067±0.0063 / -0.2145±0.0103 / +0.0028±0.0071 / -0.0433±0.0110, matching the paper's -0.207/-0.214/+0.003/-0.043 exactly) and the §3.3 decomposition (non-deferred acc 0.677→0.773, deferred acc 0.495, 45.5% deferred share all reproduce)
- The deferred-round decomposition in §3.3 is a genuine analytical improvement over the prior revision: it replaces a narrated hypothesis with an algebraic derivation (P(user correct | disagree) = 0.5 under symmetric competence) that is verified against the simulation output, and the paper explicitly revises its own earlier claim rather than just re-asserting it
- The revision is unusually transparent about what remains unresolved: §4 and §5 explicitly flag that the competence-gap assumption is still a "plausibility check, not validation" and that trust-update/reliance/confidence parameters are hand-set rather than fit to data, rather than papering over these gaps with confident language
weaknesses:
- The core contribution remains an entirely simulated, hand-parameterized model with no human-subject or human-LLM transcript data anywhere in the paper (acknowledged explicitly in §5); every number in the results is therefore a property of the authors' chosen functional forms (sigmoid reliance rule, linear trust update, Beta-like confidence means) rather than an empirically grounded finding about real sycophancy or real trust dynamics — this caps how much can be concluded about deployed systems regardless of how thorough the internal robustness checks are
- The §4 plausibility check for the load-bearing AI>user competence assumption is qualitative and hand-wavy by the authors' own admission ("no single number here is drawn from a controlled AI-vs-user-on-identical-items comparison"); this is the one assumption the entire directional result (sycophancy is harmful vs. helpful) hinges on, and it is still not measured, only gestured at via benchmark score ranges that are explicitly not decision-support accuracy
- The sensitivity sweep (§3.2), while now multi-seed, still only varies the model's own hand-set constants within ranges the authors chose (e.g. LR from 0.04-0.30, confidence gaps 0.10-0.45); this checks internal robustness of the mechanism but cannot check whether the functional forms themselves (e.g., a logistic reliance rule, linear trust update) are the right description of real human trust dynamics, so "nine perturbations survive" is a weaker claim than it may first appear
questions:
1. Given that the entire directional conclusion depends on which side of the competence gap a deployment falls on, and §4 acknowledges this is unmeasured, would the paper's contribution be better framed as a conditional/testable hypothesis paper rather than one with a title asserting sycophancy "erodes trust" as a general finding?
2. Have the authors considered fitting the reliance sigmoid and trust-update rate to any existing published human-automation trust dataset (even outside sycophancy specifically, e.g. classic automation-reliance experiments) to at least anchor the functional form, rather than the constants alone?
3. The equal-competence accuracy cost is shown to be a mechanical artifact of conditioning on disagreement (§3.3) — does this same 50%-accuracy-on-disagreement mechanism also explain part of the much larger base-configuration accuracy gap, or is that regime dominated by a different effect? A brief comparison would clarify whether the decomposition generalizes beyond the equal-competence case.
